segments.text: Imagine a local operation that raises TimeoutError twice and succeeds on its
third call.
We want to retry because the failures might be temporary.
Now imagine a different operation that raises ValueError because its input is
invalid.
Should we also call that repeatedly?
The answer should be no: repeating a permanent bad input usually does not
repair it.
In this lesson, every operation is an injected local callable, so we can
practice retry logic without touching a network or waiting in real time.
Our result will have a maximum number of attempts, a clear list of retryable
exception types, and an exponential delay schedule passed to a testable callback.
A timeout means an operation did not finish within its configured limit; a
connection error means a transport failed before a useful result.
Both may be transient, but retrying forever is dangerous.
This lesson accepts a local callable that either returns a value or raises
TimeoutError or ConnectionError.
It makes at most max_attempts calls.
Between attempts it passes a calculated delay to an injected wait callback, which
lets us test the schedule without sleeping or contacting a network.
The actual operation remains responsible for its own timeout setting; this wrapper
reacts to the TimeoutError it raises.
The first program catches Exception, the broad base class for ordinary Python
errors.
Its fake operation raises ValueError once, then returns ready.
The wrapper prints a retry message and ultimately appears successful.
This is a misleading outcome: the initial error described invalid input, not a
transient transport issue.
The example is deliberately small enough to expose the policy mistake.
In production, a broad retry can hide a KeyError, TypeError, or authentication
problem and consume extra resources without helping the user.
A retry decision is not just a loop control choice; it is a claim about which
failures could plausibly improve later.
The broken retry loop catches every Exception.
A ValueError from invalid input gets retried even though repeating the same bad
input will not fix it.
A broad handler can also hide programming errors such as a wrong key or type.
The demonstration uses a fake operation that raises ValueError once and then
returns a value; the broken wrapper reports apparent success.
That result is misleading because the first error should have been surfaced.
We will print every call and distinguish a transient failure from a permanent
application failure before deciding what the wrapper is allowed to catch.
The diagnosis lists TimeoutError, ConnectionError, and ValueError with an
explicit retryable flag.
We choose the first two for this exercise.
A timeout may indicate a slow operation, and a connection error may indicate a
temporary link failure.
Even these are not guaranteed to recover, which is why max_attempts matters.
ValueError represents an invalid application input and passes through
immediately.
Be careful with wording: our wrapper does not create a timeout or cancel a long-
running operation.
The injected operation must enforce its own timeout and raise TimeoutError.
This wrapper only handles that signal after it occurs.
Catch only TimeoutError and ConnectionError.
After a caught failure, if the current call was the last allowed attempt, re-
raise that failure.
Otherwise calculate base_delay times two to the power of the zero-based attempt
number.
With base_delay 0.5 and three attempts, the waits are 0.5 then 1.0 seconds in the
abstract schedule.
The injected wait function records those values during practice, so nothing
actually sleeps.
In a real service you may add jitter and a maximum delay to avoid many clients
retrying together; this compact lesson isolates the bounded exponential idea.
The fixed function validates its policy and loops over a bounded range.
It returns immediately on success.
When a retryable exception appears, it re- raises on the last allowed attempt.
On a nonfinal failure it calculates base_delay times two to the attempt index,
then passes that number to wait.
With base delay half a second and three attempts, the waits recorded are half a
second and one second.
The demo uses list.append as the wait callback, so the explanation can show
precise numbers without sleeping.
In a real service, you might provide a sleeping callback and add a maximum delay
and jitter; that is a separate operational decision.
The control flow is intentionally narrow.
Parameter validation happens before the first operation call, so invalid retry
settings do not partly execute work.
A successful operation returns directly.
The except tuple catches only the two chosen transient signals.
If the loop is at its final index, a bare raise preserves the original failure for
the caller.
Otherwise, the callback receives an exponentially increasing delay.
The callback is injected rather than hardcoded to time.sleep, which lets a
deterministic test record the schedule and lets other callers choose a different
policy.
Because the operation itself owns timeout enforcement, this wrapper never falsely
promises to stop a call that is still running.
The final run verifies two important boundaries.
A ValueError is surfaced after one call, with no retries and no waits.
A TimeoutError that persists through the limit is surfaced after exactly two calls
in that test, with one wait between them and no pointless wait afterward.
Also try an operation that succeeds immediately; the wait list should stay
empty.
Set max_attempts to zero, True, or 1.5, or base_delay to a negative number, and
confirm ValueError.
These checks make the retry policy observable.
On the lesson page, complete the function and use the quiz to explain why catching
every exception is unsafe and why the number of waits is one less than the
number of attempted calls in a fully failing run.
Validation is part of reliability.
Reject max_attempts unless it is a positive integer (bool and float are
invalid), and reject negative base_delay, because silent loops with zero calls or
negative waits are not meaningful.
The verification run checks a permanent ValueError is attempted only once and that
exhausted transient retries surface the final TimeoutError.
It also checks that wait is never called after the final failure or after immediate
success.
Retrying is an operational policy, not a substitute for validating inputs or
handling an API's nonretryable status.
The later offline API client project combines this policy with response
parsing, still using only fake local transport.
